paras: The Warrior miners' armed standoff was a confrontation at Warrior, Alabama, reported in June 1888, in which Black miners and white men armed themselves against each other. According to the only account, the miners armed over a grievance against their white bosses, the white men answered in kind, and bloodshed 'seemed imminent'; no violence or outcome was reported.

The dispute arose, in the account's words, from 'some supposed offense of the white bosses' at Warrior, a mining place in Alabama. The item does not say what the offense was, which mine was involved, or how many men were employed there.

The 'negro miners,' the report said, 'recently armed themselves with the intention of killing the first white man who molests them.' The white men then 'decided on the same course,' so that, by the report's account, bloodshed 'seemed imminent.' The account ends there, giving no date, no names and no numbers for either group.
No follow-up report appears in the coverage, so whether shots were fired, arrests made or the dispute settled is not known.

The episode reached print as a single sentence in a syndicated column of Southern briefs headed 'Southern Gleanings,' which The West Tennessee Star of Bolivar ran on June 22, 1888. The Huntsville Gazette, the St. Landry Democrat of Louisiana and the Grenada Sentinel of Mississippi carried the same column, with identical wording, the next day. In each paper the item sat among unrelated notices of quarrels, accidents, appointments and a Florida lynching, without a headline or comment of its own.
The column named the men only as 'negro miners' and treated their grievance as a 'supposed offense,' while it gave the white men's arming no stated reason beyond following 'the same course.'

record_check.dossier: A labor-related armed standoff between Black miners and white men; no lynching or mob attack reported
No threat against a particular person or prisoner; both sides armed with a conditional intent to kill anyone of the other race who 'molests' them
No county is named in the June coverage; only 'Warrior, Ala.'
'Recently' before 1888-06-22; it could be earlier than June
The miners threatened by the white men were Black ('negro miners'); no one was harmed
Two armed groups: Black miners and 'the white men', neither named nor counted
One syndicated item run by at least four papers, 1888-06-22 to 1888-06-23

info: The miners acted over 'some supposed offense of the white bosses'; the offense is not described

Not reported; the item ends with bloodshed 'seemed imminent'
